# OF THE WINDS.

2. <term>Procellæ</term> <gloss>Storms</gloss>, which occur with mist or darkness, which they call <term>Belluas</term> <gloss>Beasts</gloss>, and which sustain themselves like a Column, are very violent and dreadful for sailors.

3. Greater <term>Typhones</term> <gloss>Typhoons</gloss>, which seize things across a notable width and suck what is seized upwards, rarely occur; but small and almost playful <term>Vortices</term> <gloss>eddies</gloss> or <term>Turbines</term> <gloss>whirlwinds</gloss> occur frequently.

4. All <term>Procellæ</term> <gloss>Storms</gloss>, <term>Typhones</term> <gloss>Typhoons</gloss>, and larger <term>Turbines</term> <gloss>Whirlwinds</gloss> have a manifest downward motion of falling or vibration, more so than other Winds; so that they seem to rush in the manner of torrents, and flow down as if through channels, and are afterwards reflected back from the earth.

5. It happens in meadows that haystacks are sometimes carried high up and then scattered like a <term>Conopæi</term> <gloss>canopy</gloss>; likewise in fields, tangled pea stalks, the ears of harvested crops, and even linens set out to dry are lifted by <term>Turbines</term> <gloss>whirlwinds</gloss> to the height of trees or above the roofs of houses; and these things happen without any greater force or violence of the Wind.

6. But sometimes light and very narrow <term>Turbines</term> <gloss>whirlwinds</gloss> occur even in clear weather; so that a rider might see dust or straw snatched...

<summary>Bacon describes various types of sudden and violent winds, including column-like storms at sea and whirlwinds that lift light objects like hay or straw high into the air.</summary>
